builder_plan.scenario: You already need task-specific training and want to reduce its memory or compute cost.
builder_plan.change: Change only the training technique on a small controlled run after checking prerequisites.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current training recipe with the same model, data split, and evaluation.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Held-out quality, peak memory, training time, and full compute cost to the target quality.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: What's in a Tree ? Hierarchical $n$-gram models as controlled approximators of language
summary: Tree-grams replace deep transformers as the object of study with a hierarchical n-gram model whose context length n and rank d give explicit, interpretable control over horizon and capacity, used here to generate simpler synthetic data for more robust μP hyperparameter transfer and to study fine-tuning gaps via entropy and correlation range. The cost is that these are n-gram tensor models whose conditional probability structure grows with context order, so they are viable only as small-scale proxies and do not deliver production-grade language modeling despite being reported 'competitive' with transformers on the studied benchmarks. What can fail after adoption is that conclusions drawn from tree-gram surrogates, including μP transfer tuned on generated data, may not transfer to real corpora and real transformer training, since the paper's own framing is that relevance to realistic language data remains underexplored.
rationale: Tree-grams are a research instrument for controlled approximation and small-scale μP tuning on synthetic data, not a production replacement for deployed language models, so the reader should track the findings rather than adopt the method.

claims.statement: Tree-grams replace deep transformers as the object of study with a hierarchical n-gram model whose context length n and rank d give explicit, interpretable control over horizon and capacity, used here to generate simpler synthetic data for more robust μP hyperparameter transfer and to study fine-tuning gaps via entropy and correlation range. The cost is that these are n-gram tensor models whose conditional probability structure grows with context order, so they are viable only as small-scale proxies and do not deliver production-grade language modeling despite being reported 'competitive' with transformers on the studied benchmarks. What can fail after adoption is that conclusions drawn from tree-gram surrogates, including μP transfer tuned on generated data, may not transfer to real corpora and real transformer training, since the paper's own framing is that relevance to realistic language data remains underexplored.

Routing across candidate tree topologies exhibits emergent sparsity, allowing pruning of up to 95% of topologies without significant performance change; tree-grams are also reported competitive with deep transformer LMs on the studied tasks.
